docs.dcterms_abstract: A letter written by Aphra Behn sent to her handler Mr Halsall. The letter concerns Behn's first meeting with William Scot, her desire to avoid going into Holland, which she feels would be unsafe, and her plans to meet with Scot again. The letter also states that she is running low on funds. This letter includes examples of the original numeric cipher. At the end of the letter, Behn also references the inadequacies of this cipher and her wishes to use her own.

She is scared for her life and will not travel deep into Holland and instead is waiting for Scot to visit her where she is so that they may be able to settle a means of safe correspondence. In the meantime she asks for more money to sustain her while she awaits Scot.

docs.dcterms_abstract: A letter written by Aphra Behn, transcribed from original intelligence provided by William Scot, sent to her handler Mr Halsall. The letter reports on the movements of Dutch fleets, as well as the movements of certain agents known to the English, and frequently mentioned in Behn's letters, including Henry de Fleury de Coulan (Buat), Benjamin Turly, Thomas Corney, and Joesph Bampfield. The letter discusses how Bampfield has engaged a man named Mr Hill to manage the flow of intelligence to Presbyterian contacts. In the postscript, Behn denies that a letter found written in a woman's hand is hers and warns against Thomas Corney, an English agent whom she calls a rogue.

Eng. lett. c. 328, fol. 599r (with seal and postal marks) Oriell College: May the 17th Sir. I received your letter by Mr Brace, and acknowledg my very greate engagment for the trouble I have, and am like to give you. You desire in your letter a note of what China I would have, wee are already rich enough in Broad Hat China dishes, our designe is for any other fashion to mingle with them, butt beeing nott to bee purchased without difficulty in those parts you are going to, makes us dispaire of itt. Butt if there doe Happen a sale while you are att Lisbon you will oblige mee much if you m ake mee a smale purchase, so far as you beleive my purse (whichis nott a deep one) may bee able to pay you againe, and with that some Portugall ware. My sister is your servant, and will tell you so herselfe when shee is out of the Straw, shee bid mee t ell you the Boy is to hinder her frome nothing shee formerly tooke delight in, and because shee will not bee fond, sends him a -grazing 3 miles of[f] in the Country, and then falls amaine to her Painting. Since you went hence Mr Curten has married Mistris Wood's Neice Nan Drope. Mr An: Wood so highly resents itt, whether for the loss of his bosome friend or for the Lass, I know nott, butt itt has almost Crackt his braine. Mr Ben Parry has gott a very good Parsonage nigh Windsor and is going to live with th e Bishop of Winchester, in hopes of more preferment, the former beeing the Gift of a privat Patron. Had wee knowne your Stay would have been above a Moneth in London, here is a Party of your friends in Oriell College sweare they would have laid violent h ands on you rather than you should have gone so soon. I will detaine you no longer frome whatever this finds you doing, than to wish you a happy and prosperous voyage, and a speedy returne, I am Your faithfull friend and servant AS My Husband presents you with his affectionate service I doe fancy that your Jarrs and Bottles of China may nott bee to[o] deere in Portugall and fine thin dishes. I looke upon the other as the Coarser Metall, but my skill is smale These To Mr Francis Parry Present Leave this for him with Bodleian Libraries, University of Oxford Transcription by Bruce Barker -Benfield .
